title: TC1-12315
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection on July 30, 2021.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection on July 30, 2021. The Appellant is a citizen of Ghana. He fears persecution from his father, community, and the Ghanaian authorities because of his sexual orientation as bisexual. The RPD found his claim not to be credible. Given the nature of the basis of claim, I will consider and apply the Chairperson's Guideline 9 - Proceedings Before the IRB Involving Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (SOGIE)1 in my reasons outlined below. The RPD was correct in finding the Appellant had not credibly established his basis of claim. The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is credibility.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Appellant submits in his memorandum of appeal that the RPD was unreasonable. He does not offer any specific submissions on the standard of review the RAD should apply. My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2 RPD FINDINGS

The RPD's found the Appellant had not credibly established his claim; found that the Appellant did not advise his father that he is bisexual nor was he threatened or harmed by the community because of his sexual orientation while he was in Ghana in 2017; found the Appellant embellished his claim with this testimony and, thus, find his credibility was further undermined; found his credibility to be compromised by inconsistent testimony about his relationship with T, his only same-sex partner; found the Appellant's delay in claiming protection in Canada exhibited a lack of subjective fear; his failed to make a refugee claim in Holland also exhibited a lack of subjective fear; and gave little or no probative value to the documentary evidence he filed to demonstrate his sexual orientation. APPELLANT'S GROUNDS OF APPEAL The Appellant argues the RPD erred: in its assessment of the appellant's credibility based on the comparison of his testimony to his BOC narrative; in finding his delay in leaving Ghana in 2017 does not compromise his credibility to the extent that would preclude a finding that he is a person in need of protection; in making a negative credibility finding in relation to the appellant's relationship with his partner in Holland; in its assessment of the evidence provided in support of the claim and failed to consider all of the documentary evidence; committed a reviewable error in finding the Appellant's drivers licences to be fraudulent without conducting an adequate assessment of the evidence; and in finding that the letter from XXXX XXXX had little probative value in establishing the Appellant's sexual identity.

Based on his Basis of Claim form, narrative, all the documentary evidence before me and his oral testimony given at the March 9 and July 8, 2021, at his RPD hearing, I conducted an independent assessment of the evidence to determine whether the Appellant was credible in establishing his basis of claim. The following serves as a background in this appeal.

In 2003, when the Appellant was 18 years old, he fled Ghana and went to Germany made a refugee claim. At that time, he fears being killed by his ex-girlfriend's brothers because they did not approve of him, a Muslim, dating their sister, a Christian. While there he relocated to a town called XXXX in the East of Germany. In XXXX 2014 he moved to Rotterdam, Holland. While living there he discovered he was interested in men. He met a guy named T and they dated for XXXX months. After the XXXX months, the Appellant dated a woman for around a year and a half. He returned to Ghana in XXXX 2017. While in Ghana, he met a gay man by the name of D but never entered in a relationship with D. The Appellant's father went to the Appellant's home and saw D there. After the Appellant's father's visit, the Appellant and D had more secretive meetings with D as his father did not approve of them seeing each other. In XXXX 2017, the Appellant was called to a meeting with community elders. After that meeting, he alleges to have been ostracized by the community including his home being broken into and he was beaten up in XXXX 2017. He went to the police station and told them the reason of his beating was that the local youth thought he was bisexual. He went to the hospital. The Appellant left Ghana in XXXX 2017, flying from Accra, Ghana to Amsterdam, Netherlands. On XXXX XXXX, 2017, he traveled to Rotterdam but did not claim refugee protection in the Netherlands. On XXXX XXXX, 2018, he flew from the Netherlands to Canada. The Appellant made a refugee in Canada at the end of March 2018.
The Appellant filed one new piece of evidence for RAD to consider: a) Statutory Declaration from the Appellant's mother, dated XXXX XXXX, 2021.3 The evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted

According to the Law,4 I can only accept evidence that: (i) arose after the RPD decision; or (ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.5

The Appellant submits that document a) was provided by the Appellant's mother to explain why her signature was not present on her Statutory Declaration dated March 22, 2018,6 given the RPD assigned little weight to it. He argues document a) could not have been before the RPD before the rejection of claim. It is relevant as it relates directly to the appropriate weight to be given to a piece of documentary evidence that supports his claim for refugee protection.

I accept documents a) as it postdates the RPD rejection the claim, and it relates to the RPD finding that the Appellant's mother's statutory declaration before the RPD was found to have little evidentiary weight, thereby, meeting the requirements of the law. Document a) is new as it explains why the Appellant's mother had not signed the Statutory Declaration before the RPD, it is relevant to the determinative issue of the overall credibility of the evidence. On their face value, document a) is credible as it was issued by the Superior Court of Judicature in the High Court of Justice in Accra, Ghana. I accept document a). ANALYSIS Credibility

In light of the identified ground of appeal, I have independently considered the Appellant's evidence regarding his actual and perceived sexual orientation as bisexual and whether he was targeted due to his sexual orientation and find the RPD was correct in their credibility findings. Applying the Difference, Stigma, Shame, and Harm (DSSH) model to the Appellant's testimony does not demonstrate his sexual orientation has been established supports the SOGIE Guideline

In my analysis of the Appellant's testimony, I turned to the SOGIE Guideline, according to which cultural, psychological, or other barriers are likely to explain the way the testimony is presented. In addition, I considered the possibility that the stigma associated with people with various SOGIE, or the treatment of these people in Ghana, as reported in the National Documentation Package (NDP) on Ghana, may cause some reluctance or difficulty to speak on the subject. I also considered the fact the Appellant has lived outside of Ghana for many years where being bisexual may be more acceptable than Ghana.

When I apply the DSSH model to the circumstances in this appeal, I find that the Appellant did not identify in his testimony that he was different because of his sexual orientation as a bisexual man in Ghana; he did not mentioned feeling stigmatized due to his sexual orientation other than to have the knowledge that it is not accepted in Ghana, particularly by the Muslim community he lived in, and in comparison to Ghana, gay people could interact freely in Holland where he could not say for sure it was illegal in Holland to be homosexual or bisexual, not because he personally experienced stigma because of his sexual orientation but because it's common knowledge in that country; he did not demonstrate any feeling of shame because of his sexual orientation; and there is no evidence other than this his alleged physical harm he claims to have experiences at the hands of his agents of harm because of his alleged sexual orientation that I did not find credible. All of these factors point to the Appellant not demonstrating his sexual orientation has been established according to his alleged basis of claim.

In keeping with the Guideline in section 2 that a person's understanding of their sexual orientation may change. I am also further aware of the societal attitudes in Ghana towards persons of different sexual orientations is not favorable to the Appellant if he was in fact bisexual or perceived to be. When applying the DSSH Model and assessing whether the RPD erred in finding the Appellant had not established his basis of claim, namely that he is bisexual and because of his sexual orientation could face persecution in Ghana, I agree with the RPD that the Appellant has not credibly demonstrated he is bisexual or faces persecution based on his sexual orientation.

I find the Appellant has not established he is bisexual or that he had credibly been perceived to be bisexual. The RPD was correct in concluding the RPD had not established he was bisexual. Realization of being bisexual in Holland does not establish is sexual orientation

During his testimony, the Appellant described his sexual orientation as bisexual7. He said he realized he was bisexual when he left Germany in 2014 and went to Holland.8 When responding to the RPD question, he said9 the time he realized that he was sexually attracted to both women and men was when he returned to Holland during the summertime and attended a gay festival. He liked the lifestyle, and it was there that he met T who provided support to him. T introduced him to the gay community, and it was then that he realized that gay people were not bad people.

The RPD did not make a finding on the Appellant's realization of being bisexual in general, let alone in Holland. The Appellant's evidence does not provide me with any insight of him feeling different because of his sexual orientation or other insight on when he realized he was bisexual and how that impacted him. This is an indicator that the Appellant is not bisexual.

I further note the Appellant's evidence does not raise any feeling of shame or stigma that is often associated in claims for sexual orientation in countries where being bisexual is illegal and the Muslim faith in Ghana would not support it. This is also an indicator that the Appellant is not bisexual. I will assess the harm factor in the DHSS model further in my reasons but will now turn to the evidence of the Appellant's alleged bisexual relationships in this case. Only alleged same sex relationship with T is not credible
The RPD found it unreasonable that the claimant was unable to keep his story straight regarding a significant aspect of T's sexuality. It found his credibility was compromised.

The Appellant argues that he answered numerous questions about T in an honest, forthright manner with details. He suggests a review of the audio demonstrates that he provided significant details about their relationship without hesitation, and that the "discrepancy" identified by the panel stemmed from confusion that arose in the exchange regarding timing and manner in which the appellant learned of T's sexual orientation. Accordingly, he submits that it was unreasonable for the RPD to have found that his credibility was compromised on this basis.

The Appellant identified having one same-sex relationship with a man named T in Holland in his narrative and testimony. In his narrative10 it states that he had met T when he first moved to Rotterdam, but he did not know T was gay. He found out that he was when he saw him participate in the gay festival and get dressed up which is when he realized he was homosexual. It further states that the Appellant was going through a rough time, they became good friends and T treated him with kindness and respect. He realized that the gay community in Holland is very respectful and open to others which is what attracted him to them. He said he never felt discriminated with them. He also indicates T and he dated for around XXXX months and then T met someone else. After this, I dated a woman for around a year and a half.

The Appellant also testified about his alleged relationship with T. He said they were living together the way spouses do. T was the one who prepared meals, he said "he was like the woman".11 Occasionally, they would prepare the meal together. He said T would work every day and on the weekends he would be home. The Appellant was working on and off. Together, they would visit friends, go for groceries on the weekends when they were home. When describing what he liked about T, he said that T as a very good man and the people T took him to meet where good people too. T was from the Ivory Coast. He had papers in Holland and a working authorization, he has been there a long time. When asked by the RPD why his narrative does not mention they lived together, he said by their "African understanding, when you say dating, it's like someone you are befriending, like, girlfriend, boyfriend, and it's like you -- you are together. So, that was why I did not -- it's now that you are asking for details that I'm bringing in this, but when you refer to dating, it's the same like you are together. Like in our language -- in our local language, when we refer to that, it means the same, dating and staying together".12 During the resumption of his refugee claim, the Appellant reaffirmed his relationship with T was about seven years ago and he has not had a same-sex relationship since.13 He said he spoke with a man at "XXXX XXXX" but the man did not appear interested so he did not pursue it. Lastly, he said after T, he entered into a relationship with a woman for a year and a half.14

I find T's sexual orientation is not as determinative issue for me as the RPD appeared to make it. Rather, I focused on the evidence of whether the Appellant had a same-sex relationship with T which would assist me in assessing his sexual orientation as bisexual. The evidence before me in this case regarding the Appellant's alleged same sex is not credible. I find the Appellant's evidence does not demonstrate provide me with much insight into a same-sex relationship that was allegedly a serious one whereby the Appellant and T lived together for three months. He provided little information as to what he liked about the T, other than he was a very good man, he provided no details about T's qualities, likes/dislikes, details about his job. Stating that T cooked for him because T took on the "woman role" in their relationship, in my view possibly is a stereotype that I will not associate to the SOGIE community. In support of the SOGIE Guideline, the RPD avoided stereotypes such as individuals with diverse SOGIE have feminized or masculine appearances or mannerisms which in this case,15 the Appellant described as T's feminine role. I also, will not stereotype this alleged role and find the Appellant's description of such suggests to me he has described a possible stereotype he would have about gay men. The Appellant's lacked insight into knowing T on such a personal level or any other detailed information to share for someone who allegedly lived with T for XXXX months. I acknowledge that the SOGIE Guideline does not require corroborating evidence16 and there are times when only the Appellant's evidence will be available to me,17however, the Appellant's has not demonstrated he had a same-sex relationship with T. Moreover, the Appellant has not had any other same-sex relationships since his alleged on with T which I do not find credible. This is an indicator that he is not bisexual or established his basis of claim. Heterosexual relationships established

The Appellant confirmed in his narrative and his oral testimony that he has been in longer-term relationships with women, the first was with a Christian woman before he left Ghana in 2003 for Germany, and the second, after his alleged same-sex relationship with T, was with a woman for a year and a half. These facts do not establish the Appellant credibly establishing his sexual orientation as bisexual. The Appellant's declaration to D of being bisexual is not credible

A Statutory Declaration of D dated XXXX XXXX, 2018,18 was filed in support of the Appellant's claim. According to the Appellant, D is allegedly the Appellant's friend who allegedly is homosexual. D states in his declaration that he met the Appellant in 2017 at the XXXX XXXX in Ghana. During those days of text and talk, the Appellant made it known to D that he is bisexual.

The Appellant never mentions having told D was bisexual in his narrative referred to above or his oral testimony. In fact, his testimony would lead me to believe he did not specifically admit to anyone that he was in fact bisexual but rather said to his father and Elders that he would live life as he wants to. I place no weight on D's Statutory Declaration to corroborate that the Appellant has established his sexual orientation. The Appellant is not credible about he admitted to his father that he was bisexual

The RPD found the Appellant did not advise his father that he is bisexual nor was he threatened or harmed by the community because of his sexual orientation while he was in Ghana in 2017. It found the Appellant's inability to provide a spontaneous account with some detail beyond his written narrative about critical aspects of his claim, lead me to find his credibility undermined.

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in coming to this finding. He submits that he did in fact provide a spontaneous account regarding his communications with his father and how his father learned of his sexual orientation. He submits that there is no inconsistency between him having told his father about his sexuality and his father having heard from members of the community that his son was associating with a gay man; both can be true at the same time; his communications with his father were consistent with his BOC narrative. He also submits that the omission of this death threat in the BOC narrative does not diminish the central elements of the appellant's refugee claim and is not a sufficient reason to rebut the presumption of truthfulness.

In his written narrative, the claimant alleges that he told his father that he was bisexual. The evidence in his narrative about his father finding out he was bisexual and the threats he injured once that information was in his community is the following: "Return to Ghana: XXXX 2017 20. When I arrived in Ghana, I stayed with my mother for XXXX XXXX days, but soon rented a room, also in Accra, but in a different neighbourhood than my parents. Where I lived is like a compound where several people rent small apartments / rooms. 21. Around XXXX XXXX after living in Accra, I befriended a man called D. We met playing football. I knew he was gay because of the way he dressed and he had effeminate gestures. 22. D and I became close friends. We would hang out together and he introduced me to his friends. However, D had a boyfriend so we were not intimate together. I knew we were attracted to each other but we never entered into a relationship because he never broke it off with his boyfriend, no matter how much he complained about him. 23. People in the community started to notice that I was associating with D. Either people saw that I was in his car or that he had visited me home. D had come to visit me twice at my apartment. This was towards the end of March or the beginning of April, 2017. 24. During D's second visit to my place, my father came to my apartment to speak to me. He is the Iman of our community so he is very well known. I can only assume someone informed my father than D visited me at home and this is why he came to my place. I told my father I had a visitor and if he had anything to say we could talk at a later date. Upset, my father left my place. 25. The next day, my father returned and started to scold me. He said he heard that D was gay and he did not want me to associate with him. Because in Islam it is a sin to be gay, my father used derogatory terms to speak about D, saying things like he had a "cursed lifestyle", or he is "living the low life", and calling gays "stupid people". 26. Then my dad asked if I 'practiced the same sexuality" as D and I told him I was a bisexual. I told my dad that when I was in Europe I saw the freedom over there and that people in Europe relate with who they like (such as persons from the same sex. I told him this is what my life was like over there and explained that even Arabs in Europe were free. I also told my father that I was not in a relationship with D. 27. I was afraid speaking to my father like this given the influence he has over the community, and because of his violent nature. He is very aggressive with my mother and while growing up, he used to beat me as punishment. 28. At the same time, I wanted to educate my father about the freedom I experienced in Europe. I was no longer a little boy; I had lived 14 years in Europe and had taken care of myself. I told him he was not the one supporting me in Ghana and that I wanted my freedom. I am not sure how my mother felt about the situation. In any event, she is fearful of my father so will not oppose his actions. (Emphasis added) 29. Unfortunately, I had to ask D not to come back to my apartment because of the problems it was causing. So, we would be more secretive about our meetings."19

The Appellant testified that he is afraid of his father because he was the person that sent the youth to attack him.20 He said his father is a leader in the community.21 He said22 he told his father he was bisexual because he was with his friend D, at his home, he knew that someone within the community had informed his father. He did not initially tell his father when he was knocking at the door because he told him he had a visitor. When the visitor was gone, he later told his father they would have conversation. The next day he was home, and his father came again. He said his father said he learned that from the community that D was gay and then his father asked the Appellant why he was associating or moving with that. The Appellant said he chose to tell his father of his sexual preferences. When he told his father, his father left. He father told him that that kind of lifestyle, his father did not want it. His father said it is not allowed in the Islamic or Muslim faith, He told his father because I knew he is his father, and whatever he told him he does not, or he would not go to talk to the other community members about it. That was what the Appellant told himself. When the RPD asked the Appellant to clarify why he said the community told his father, the Appellant said23 that D is not a Muslim and that D was not in his community; because he and D played soccer together and that people understand or kind of understand that D was or he is gay. The Appellant said that both he and D moved together during that time, and D visited him twice. He said he was not sure whether it was during the visit that the community saw him in his car that the community kind of suspected. The Appellant said he believe somebody must have told his dad because when D came, it was not long before his father started knocking at his door. He said he knew that within the community, somebody went and told his dad.

Based on the evidence form the Appellant, I am not convinced the Appellant actually confirmed or outright told his father he is bisexual because he does not say that, rather he describes saying he told him about his sexual preference and that he choses to live his life in freedom. In my view, the Appellant has not specifically told his father he is bisexual. Also, given the objective24 evidence of cultural and country response generally seen in Ghana against homosexuals or bisexuals, I find the Appellant's evidence that he told his Muslim father that he was bisexual and that his father just walked away not to be credible. I agree with the RPD that there are some inconsistencies in the evidence as to who told the Appellant's father first about his alleged bisexual orientation, the Appellant's father's calm reaction to finding out regardless of who told him first does not follow the expected reaction of a Muslim leader in a country where being bisexual would be illegal. I do not find the Appellant's allegation that he told his father he was bisexual to be credible. This is an indicator that he has not demonstrated he is bisexual or allegations of fear of persecution because of his sexual orientation. The community leaders alleged non-reaction to them learning the Appellant was bisexual is not credible

The RPD did not make a specific finding on the meeting the Appellant was alleged summoned after his father allegedly found out he was bisexual; however, this evidence is important and, in my opinion, equally goes to the credibility of the heart of this claim. I do not find this to be a new issue, as this is evidence in the record before me. I, therefore, do not see the need to raise the fact that I independently assessed the evidence of the elders meeting to demonstrate the Appellant's cumulative evidence is not credible in supporting his basis of claim. The RAD conducts independent assessment of the evidence considering the grounds of appeal whether the Appellant credibly established his claim is before me.

The evidence regarding the meeting which took place in XXXX 2017.25 He testified26 at the RPD hearing that he was summoned to a meeting his community leaders. That he was asked questions, he tried to talk to them and then let them know that as he lives his life, he does not bother anyone. He said he knew his father had told them something. And he told them that it's his life, he does not bother anybody. He said they became angry when he said that. He said he told them that okay, he's going somewhere then he left. After his meeting with the community leader, the youth told him that he should leave the community.

Again, the reaction of the Muslim community leaders or the general country response is not what I would have expected based on the Objective evidence in the Ghana NDP.27 Like the reaction from the Appellant's father, according to his testimony, the community leaders summoned him to then let him go after despite being angry and no other consequences. This makes no sense to me and, therefore, I do not find the Muslim leaders' reaction to the Appellant essentially stating it's his life and he will live his life as he wishes not to get a different reaction, such as a mob attack then and there. Based on the objective evidence, people who are SOGIE have no choice but to deny who they are, the fact that the Appellant was open to doing so in Ghana, even despite him being away in Europe for several years who may be more tolerant of different people's sexual orientation, knowing the country's views on homosexuality the Appellant's version that he easily told his community leaders and no immediate repercussions ensued is not credible. This is another indication that the Appellant's basis of claim is not credibly established. The Appellant is not credible that he was threatened or harmed because of sexual orientation

I find the supporting evidence filed by the Appellant does not, on a balance of probabilities, establish that the physical altercation he experiences in XXXX 2017, was because of his sexual orientation. The evidence that supports my conclusion is evaluated below.

The RPD found the Appellant omitted in his narrative a specific threat to kill him which is a material fact of his claim. It found the Appellant embellished his claim with this testimony and, thus, found his credibility was further undermined. Given the Appellant's arguments at appeal, the RPD also found the Police Diary Extract and other documentary evidence either had no weight or no probative value to demonstrate his sexual orientation or that that he was attacked as alleged.

The Appellant does not provide specific arguments about this omission but submitted that the RPD erred in assessing the Appellant's oral testimony and documentary evidence that supported his claim. I agree with the RPD that the Appellant omitted in his narrative a specific threat to kill him which is a material fact to his claim. However, I will assess the other evidence about his attack and sexual orientation to determine if the RPD erred in placing no weight to support his basis of claim. The Appellant's narrative and oral evidence does not credibly establish he was beaten due to his sexual orientation.

The Appellant's narrative indicates that his home was broken in which led to his being beaten. The attack, police reporting of the attack and medical attention he received were specified in his narrative as follows: "41. Then , when I was in the compound (which all our rooms encircle) I saw many young men approach me. Some were holding sticks and some had weapons (machetes). Then, they started to hit me with their sticks and one guy cut my hand with his knife. They pushed me to the concrete floor. I was all alone as the neighbors were too afraid to come out. 42. When the Youth were assaulting me, they said they had warned me and threatened me but I was not listening. They said they had told me to leave the community, but I had not left. 43. Then, a neighbor called Mr. R came out of his room and the Youth ran away. Mr. R insisted that the incident should be reported to the police so we drove to the station. 44. At the station, the police noticed there was blood on my arm so they asked me what happened and about the motive of the aggressors. I told them the Youth thought I was bisexual. I was not afraid to say this to the police because they did not have evidence that I was interested in men. I only said that the Youth believed I was bisexual. 45. The Police suggested I go seek medical attention and then asked me to return on the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2017. 46. At the Hospital, the doctor asked me the reason why I was attacked and I explained to him it was because the Youth suspected I was bisexual. Even though same sex relations are prohibited in Ghana, I was not afraid that I would get in trouble for saying this as I had said I was suspected of being bisexual, not that I was actually bisexual. The doctor was sympathetic and told me the Youth were wrong to attack someone on a mere suspicion. I stayed at the hospital for around XXXX hours as the doctor attended to my wounds." (Emphasis added) ... 47. Around XXXX months after I was beaten for being bisexual, the area boys started to threaten me again. For instance, when I would be walking in the neighborhood, they would block my path. The guys would tell me: ·'We have warned you, but you are still here. One day we will beat you until death".28

The Appellant testified that he was attacked on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, about a month after the Elders meeting.29 The Appellant testified about this incident and that he reported the attack to the police. He said he was afraid that that the police will attack him because of his sexual orientation and that because if he was attacked or when he was there, and he made any report to the police of the attack, they too will get him locked up.30 At the hearing resumption, he testified: "When I went in, I was -- I was --- When I went in, I was wondering what was happening, and then some youth came in and when they came in, I was wondering what happened. And then there, they started attacking me. There one of them with a stick hit me and then for me to turn and look, one of them used a knife to attack me. And there I was yelling, or I was screaming for help, and within the neighborhood, people are afraid of those youth. And they were -- as they were beating me, they said, they had given me warning that I should leave that community before. And then -- and then they beat me and then I fall on the concrete, and I -- as I was there, one neighbor opened the door, and then when they saw the door open, they run away. He was the one that took me and said, no, this thing is too much. Let's report it to the police."31 He also said32 that after that, he went to look for an earning. Most of the time, he went out to work and then he would come back home in the evening. He said he then received other threats in XXXX, that was when he decided to leave. It was in XXXX that he decided he wanted to leave.

The Appellant's evidence is generally corroborated between his narrative and testimony, however, when considering what he alleges happened in Ghana, reported to the police and despite testifying he had subsequent threats all of a sudden in XXXX 2017 which allegedly led to him having to leave Ghana, I do not find his allegation that he was allegedly beaten in XXXX 2017 because of his sexual orientation to being left alone for the youth to come back in XXXX to threaten him against again because of his alleged sexual orientation. If I was to believe he was beaten by the youth in his community because of his sexual orientation in XXXX 2017, then I would have expected him to have continued to receive threats or other attacks, yet this did not happen. I also do not believe he was threatened because of his alleged bisexuality in XXXX which resulted in him needing to leave Ghana because of his alleged sexual orientation. I do not find the Appellant has credibly established the attack occurred because of his alleged sexual orientation or that he was perceived to be bisexual by his community. I also do not believe that the Appellant would not be afraid of the Ghana police as he so indicated in his narrative (area emphasized) given its illegal to be homosexual or in this case bisexual in Ghana as per the objective evidence. The fact that the Appellant did not seem to be bothered by someone even believing him to be bisexual calls into question his credibility about his sexual orientation. As such, I considering the harm factor in the DSSH model, I do not find the Appellant was harmed because of his alleged sexual orientation. By not finding that such incident occurred, this is another indicator that he has not established his basis of claim. The Ghana Police Extract from Station Diary and General Medical Form does not establish the attack on the Appellant was because of his alleged sexual orientation

The Appellant filed a Ghana Police Extract from Station Diary33 to corroborate the break in and the beating he alleged he received because of his sexual orientation. The Extract from Station Diary and Medical Form are dated XXXX XXXX, 2017. In the Extract from Station Diary,34 the Ghana Police records the Appellant's complaint about his house being broken into and his pet being killed. It refers to six guys with cutlasses and sticks coming directly to his door. He said he was told by them that until he stops being bisexual, they are going to make his life miserable. They beat him with stick and slaps on the floor. His neighbours were scared to come close until the guys left. His neighbour, Mr. R brought him to the police station to make a report. He told the police that his left hand is hurting so serious that he thought he needed medical attention. The Ghana Police Medical Form35 is a referral to any Government Hospital and highlights that the Appellant complains that he/she was "under mob attack due to him bring a bisexual."

Though the Appellant testified that he told the Ghana Police that the youth "thought" or "suspected" he was bisexual as previously indicated, the Ghana Police Extract from Diary does not state that. In his narrative where I emphasized above, he used the words "suspect of being" bisexual, the same language was referred to. Despite the Appellant claiming to fear report to the Police because of his sexual orientation, if his sexual orientation was credibly established this would be correct, however, he has not reconciled why he did go to the Ghana police despite fearing being arrested because it's illegal to be homosexual in Ghana. Also, the Ghana Police General Medical Form explicitly states the Appellant complained he was under attack due to him being a bisexual. I do not have an actual medical report from any hospital in Ghana to support he was treated for the injuries he alleges. I further note that the only injury the Appellant reported to the Police is an injured hand, yet he claims to have been beating by six men with cutlasses and sticks. The alleged attack and resulting self-reported injuries are not credible. I place no weight on the Ghana Police Extract for the purpose of credibly establishing that the Appellant was in fact attacked and beaten due to his sexual orientation because this attack was self-reported and given the confirmed information that the Police receiving from the Appellant that he alleged acknowledgement that he was bisexual as noted in their reports, the consequences of such do not match the outcome. On one hand, the Appellant appears to understand that admitting he is bisexual to the Ghana police could cause him to be arrested yet, on the other hand, he did so as reported by the Police report before me, and yet he faced no consequences. For these reasons, I do not find the Ghana Police documents credible and place no weight on them. This is an indicator that this alleged attack did not happen because of his alleged sexual orientation. The Appellant's mother's statutory declarations do not overcome credibility concerns

The Appellant's mother's statutory declaration before the RPD that it gave no weight and had issue with the fact that it had not been signed was also considered. Also, I have document a) which addresses why the initial mother's statutory declaration was not signed, namely because she does not write. I accept the fact that the Appellant's mother does not write and, therefore her statutory declaration dated XXXX XXXX, 2018, is not signed. I turn to the Appellant's statutory declaration and still find it does not assist me in overcoming the credibility concerns in this appeal. More specifically, while his mother indicates36 that her son is bisexual and that her husband, the Appellant's father, told her so; that the elders cautioned him once and he was threatened that if he does not stop the act, he will be "punish" severally and that bisexual in Islam is death; she declares he was one beaten by the youths of the community and he got hurt on the left "haed". I find the Appellant's mother's statutory declaration does not overcome the credibility concerns already addressed in this appeal. Again, her own declaration of the fact that bisexual is death supports my conclusion that his father, an Islam leader, and the Islam community leaders, would not have just cautioned him and let him go without consequences. I also note the injuries she mentions is misspelled, despite her being illiterate, the document is from the courts and has errors. I will not speculate on what part of the body his mother refers to him injuring himself as its not determinative in my view given my previous comments about the alleged injuries he sustained. For these reasons, I place no weight on the Appellant's mother's declaration to demonstrate his basis of claim. More specifically, I find her declaration weights against the threat and attack attacking due to his sexual orientation. Summary

I find the RPD correctly found the Appellant has not credibly established his basis of claim and that he is or would be perceived to be bisexual in Ghana. As such, the Appellant has not demonstrated that he would face persecution due to his sexual orientation and not established that there is a serious possibility of persecution, or that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant would be personally exposed to the risk of being subjected to torture, a threat to his life or the risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to Ghana.

Though the RPD made findings on delay in claiming and other conclusions not to find the Appellant's documentary evidence to hold any weight or probative value and the Appellant has argued that the RPD was unreasonable in coming to those conclusions, in my view, I have addressed the determinative issues and need not go any further. I have also considered entirety of the evidence before me and find even his attendance at XXXX XXXX as he submitted was not considered by the RPD would not be an error because it does not establish his sexual orientation, it does not go to the heart of his claim, and it does not overcome the cumulative credibility concerns identified.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
